title: AI Code Security Scanning — Snyk, Semgrep & the SAST Reality Check

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Lesson 9-11 covered independent PR-review bots — CodeRabbit, Graphite, Greptile — that check whether a pull request is well-written: logic errors, missed edge cases, style, maintainability. This lesson covers a genuinely different function that happens to sit in a similar place in your workflow: **SAST (Static Application Security Testing)** — tools like Snyk and Semgrep that scan code specifically for known vulnerability *patterns* (SQL injection, hardcoded secrets, insecure deserialization, the OWASP Top 10) rather than general code quality. By the end you'll understand what these tools do well, what a real, sobering set of independent benchmarks says they still miss, and why AI-generated code has its own distinct blind spots that a default ruleset won't catch. You'll finish having run a real scan on real code and reviewed its findings with informed skepticism rather than blind trust.

## A Different Function From Lesson 9-11's Review Bots

CodeRabbit, Graphite, and Greptile read a diff and reason about it holistically — does this logic make sense, does this handle the edge case, is this maintainable. SAST tools work differently: they pattern-match (or, increasingly, semantically analyze) code against a library of known vulnerability signatures and data-flow rules — does user input reach a SQL query without sanitization, does this response include a header that enables XSS, is there a hardcoded API key in this file. One checks whether the code is *good*; the other checks whether the code is *exploitable* in a specific, catalogued way. Plenty of teams run a PR-review bot, a SAST scanner, and a human reviewer simultaneously, because each is checking for a different failure mode and none of them substitutes for either of the others.

## Semgrep — Pattern Matching, Now With AI Triage

Semgrep ships three products: Semgrep Code (SAST), Semgrep Supply Chain (SCA with reachability analysis), and Semgrep Secrets. The core SAST engine exists in two tiers — an open-source Community Edition and a proprietary Pro engine with cross-file analysis — and it's fast, typically scanning a medium-sized codebase in under 30 seconds, because it's built on pattern matching rather than full compilation.

Semgrep's 2026 AI layer is **Semgrep Assistant**, which handles automated triage rather than detection itself: it filters SAST noise by analyzing code context and historical triage decisions, with Semgrep reporting roughly 96% alignment with human triage calls, and a "Memories" feature that learns from a team's past true-positive/false-positive judgments so the same pattern isn't re-flagged every scan. Semgrep's custom rule engine — supporting metavariables, taint tracking, and inter-procedural analysis that mirrors your target language's own syntax — is widely considered the strongest in the category, which matters directly for the AI-blind-spot problem covered later in this lesson: a team that tunes its own rules can close gaps a generic default ruleset leaves open.

## Snyk — Semantic Analysis and Agentic Fixes

Snyk Code's SAST engine, DeepCode AI, processes code server-side and builds a semantic "code graph" that traces data flows across files rather than reading each file in isolation. Snyk's 2026 platform push is "Agentic Fixes": autonomous agents that don't just flag a vulnerability but perform reachability triage — attempting to confirm a flagged issue is actually exploitable in this codebase's real call paths before surfacing it — plus as-you-type scanning and auto-fix suggestions Snyk reports at 80%+ accuracy. Snyk supports 30-plus languages and frameworks, and — because it started as a software composition analysis (SCA) tool and added SAST later, the reverse of Semgrep's origin story — it tends to be the stronger choice when you also need dependency and container scanning under one platform, not just first-party code.

**The reality check: independent testing paints a much less flattering picture than either vendor's own marketing.** The most rigorous academic benchmark available, from EASE 2024 (the ACM International Conference on Evaluation and Assessment in Software Engineering), tested four SAST tools against 170 manually curated commits with known, real vulnerabilities in production Java code. Run with default rule sets, **all four tools combined detected only 38.8% of the known vulnerabilities — meaning 61.2% went undetected by every single tool tested.** Notably, in that specific independent benchmark, Snyk Code had the *lowest* detection rate of the four tools, despite marketing language emphasizing its semantic code-graph analysis. A separate real-world test against 26 known vulnerabilities found Snyk caught 10 of 26 and Semgrep caught fewer than half, with both showing very limited coverage of the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications specifically. None of this means these tools are worthless — a scanner that catches 40% of real vulnerabilities for a few minutes of CI time is still worth running — but it means a clean scan is evidence of *reduced* risk, not evidence of *no* risk, and should never be read as a green light on its own.

## AI-Generated Code Has Its Own Distinct Blind Spots

A 2026 report from DryRun Security is worth taking seriously precisely because it wasn't a contrived security test. Researchers tasked three coding agents — Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6, OpenAI Codex with GPT-5.2, and Google Gemini 2.5 Pro — with building two realistic applications from ordinary product specifications, with no security guidance added to the prompts. Across 38 scans covering 30 pull requests, the agents produced 143 security issues; **26 of the 30 PRs — 87% — contained at least one vulnerability.**

The pattern that matters most for this lesson: many of the vulnerabilities were **logic and authorization flaws that regex-based, pattern-matching SAST tools structurally cannot see.** A traditional scanner flags a known-bad function call or string pattern — it does not trace whether authentication middleware is actually mounted on every route, whether an authorization check applies uniformly across every connection type, or whether a cost or quantity validation genuinely happens server-side rather than only in client-side code that a scanner never runs. Claude's agent in that study introduced a 2FA-disable bypass none of the other agents produced and carried an unauthenticated destructive endpoint from an early PR all the way to the project's end — the longest-lived unresolved finding in the study. Two other recurring blind spots showed up across independent security research on AI-generated code specifically: **hardcoded example credentials** left over from scaffolding or boilerplate the model generated (which pass a SAST scan because they look structurally like valid code, not because they're safe), and **missing input validation**, which the same research attributes partly to a real structural limitation — an AI model generating one function at a time often can't perform the deep, whole-codebase data-flow analysis needed to know which inputs are trusted and which are hostile.

## Tuning Rulesets for AI-Specific Patterns

The practical response isn't to distrust SAST tools less or more in the abstract — it's to recognize that a default, general-purpose ruleset was built for human-written code's typical mistakes, and AI-generated code has a shifted mistake profile: insecure defaults, unvalidated inputs left un-flagged because they look syntactically fine, and silent error suppression. Teams getting real value from SAST on AI-generated code are the ones actively tuning rules toward these specific patterns rather than accepting out-of-the-box defaults — which is exactly where Semgrep's strong custom-rule support (from earlier in this lesson) earns its keep. Pair SAST with dedicated secrets scanning (TruffleHog, GitLeaks) rather than assuming your SAST tool's built-in secrets detection is comprehensive, and treat SCA/dependency scanning as a separate concern entirely — AI coding assistants have been documented hallucinating package names that attackers then register ("slopsquatting"), a supply-chain risk that bypasses SCA tools completely because the malicious package, once squatted, genuinely exists.

**This is one more layer, not a replacement for the layers before it.** Lesson 9-11 already established that PR-review bots don't replace human review on high-stakes code — authentication, financial calculations, regulated data. The same rule applies here, with more force given this lesson's numbers: a SAST scan that misses 60%+ of known vulnerability patterns, on top of AI-generated code's own additional blind spots in logic and authorization, is a genuinely useful automated first pass — not a substitute for a human who understands what the code is actually supposed to do and checks whether it does that safely.

sections.title: Workshop 1 — Run a Real SAST Scan and Judge Its Findings Honestly
sections.content:
**Goal:** run Semgrep or Snyk on a real repository — ideally one containing AI-generated code from earlier in this course — and evaluate what it catches and what it plausibly misses.

**Step 1 — Install a scanner.** Semgrep: `pip install semgrep` or `brew install semgrep` (free, no account needed for the Community ruleset). Snyk: `npm install -g snyk` and `snyk auth` (free tier available).

**Step 2 — Pick a real repository you control** — one of the projects you've built with Claude Code, Copilot, or another AI tool earlier in this course is ideal, since it puts this lesson's AI-blind-spot discussion in front of code that was actually AI-generated.

**Step 3 — Run the scan:** `semgrep --config=auto .` or `snyk code test`. Read every finding, not just the ones that sound alarming.

**Step 4 — For each finding, judge it explicitly:** genuine vulnerability, false positive, or real-but-low-priority? Note which ones you're confident a human reviewer would have caught anyway, and which ones you're glad the scanner caught.

**Step 5 — Now hunt for what it *didn't* catch.** Deliberately check the two blind spots this lesson named: search the codebase for any hardcoded example credential, token, or password left over from scaffolding, and check one or two endpoints or functions for missing input validation on untrusted data. Note whether the scanner flagged either one.

**Outcome:** a real scan of real code, a written judgment on each finding, and a concrete answer — not a hypothetical — to whether this scanner would have caught this lesson's two named AI-specific blind spots in your own project.

sections.question: A team already runs CodeRabbit (lesson 9-11) on every pull request. A security engineer proposes also adding Semgrep. A developer objects that this is redundant — "we already have AI reviewing every PR." What's the most accurate response, based on this lesson?
options: The developer is right — running both tools checks the same thing twice and wastes CI time

CodeRabbit and Semgrep check for genuinely different things — CodeRabbit reasons about whether the code is well-written (logic, edge cases, maintainability), while Semgrep pattern-matches against known vulnerability signatures (injection, hardcoded secrets, insecure data flows) — and neither substitutes for the other or for human review on high-stakes code
Semgrep should replace CodeRabbit entirely since security scanning is strictly more valuable than code-quality review
Neither tool is worth running since independent benchmarks show SAST tools miss the majority of known vulnerabilities anyway
sections.explanation: This lesson opens by drawing exactly this distinction: PR-review bots and SAST scanners are a different function, not a redundant one — one checks whether code is well-written, the other checks whether it's exploitable in a specific, catalogued way. The EASE 2024 finding that SAST tools miss a majority of vulnerabilities (D) is a real, important caveat from this lesson, but it argues for treating SAST as one useful, imperfect layer among several (paired with review bots, human review, and tuned rulesets) — not for skipping it. Neither tool should replace the other (A, C) — they're complementary layers, the same conclusion 9-11 reached about PR bots and human review.

sections.title: Workshop 2 — Write Your Team's AI-Code Security Review Policy
sections.content:
**Goal:** produce a concrete, written policy for what security review AI-generated code must pass before merging — grounded in this lesson's actual numbers, not an assumption that a passing scan means safe code.

**Step 1 — List the layers you'd actually require** for code an AI tool helped write: SAST scan (which tool, what ruleset), secrets scanning, dependency/SCA scanning, PR-review bot, required human review — and for which categories of change each layer is mandatory versus optional.

**Step 2 — Name your high-stakes categories explicitly** — authentication, authorization, payment or financial logic, anything touching regulated data — and state plainly that a passing automated scan is never sufficient on its own for these, echoing lesson 9-11's warning callout.

**Step 3 — Address this lesson's two named AI blind spots directly:** what specific check (manual or tuned-rule) catches a hardcoded example credential left in scaffolding? What check catches missing server-side input validation that a default SAST ruleset would pass over?

**Step 4 — Ask Claude.ai to stress-test your policy:** *"Here's my team's security review policy for AI-generated code: [paste Steps 1-3]. Given that independent benchmarks show SAST tools miss 50-60%+ of known vulnerabilities and AI-generated code has distinct blind spots in logic and authorization, what gap in this policy would let a real vulnerability through?"*

**Step 5 — Save the finished policy** somewhere your team would actually reference it before merging AI-assisted code.

**Outcome:** a written, stress-tested security review policy for AI-generated code — not a vague intention to "scan for vulnerabilities," but a concrete set of required layers with named tools and named exceptions.

sections.question: A developer runs Semgrep on a feature an AI coding agent just built, gets zero findings, and merges immediately. Based on this lesson's EASE 2024 benchmark and the DryRun Security 2026 study, what's the most accurate assessment of that decision?
options: This is correct practice — a clean SAST scan is strong evidence the code is free of security vulnerabilities

A clean scan reduces risk but is not evidence of safety on its own — the EASE 2024 benchmark found four SAST tools combined missed 61.2% of known vulnerabilities in real code with default rules, and 87% of PRs in the DryRun study contained a vulnerability despite being built by capable, current-generation coding agents, with many being logic/authorization flaws that pattern-matching SAST tools structurally can't detect
SAST scans are only useful for code written by humans, not AI-generated code, so running Semgrep here was pointless
The developer should have used Snyk instead, since Snyk always outperforms Semgrep
sections.explanation: This lesson's core reality check is exactly this: a clean SAST result is not a green light. The EASE 2024 study found the combined detection rate across four tools with default rules was only 38.8% — meaning most real vulnerabilities in the test set went uncaught by all four. Separately, the DryRun Security 2026 study found 87% of PRs built by capable current-generation coding agents contained at least one vulnerability, and many were logic/authorization flaws outside what pattern-matching SAST can see at all. SAST tools are useful on both human and AI-generated code (C is wrong), and the independent EASE 2024 benchmark specifically found Snyk had the lowest detection rate of the four tools tested, contradicting any claim that it 'always outperforms' Semgrep (D is wrong).

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 9-14 — and Part 9's full tour of the AI coding tool landscape.** From in-editor assistants (Copilot, Continue.dev in Part 6) through autonomous cloud agents (Devin, Codex CLI, Jules), independent PR-review bots (CodeRabbit, Greptile, Graphite), open-source agentic editors (Cline, Roo Code), AWS's spec-driven Kiro, and now the SAST reality check in this lesson, you've built a grounded, current map of this space — including its genuine limits, not just its marketing. Part 7 goes all-in on Claude Code, the tool this course uses for everything from here forward — and you now carry a healthy, evidence-based skepticism about any single tool's claims into how you use it.
